# Introduction

## Context

Migration barriers and habitat fragmentation are the main threats impacting freshwater and diadromous fish species globally [@belletti2020]. Though barrier removal is often the preferred course of action, it is not always feasible because of economical or safety-related reasons. Potential other solutions to promote fish movement include fish passes and fish elevators, though there efficiency is often strongly dependent on the local conditions and target species [@noonan2012]. Therefore these systems need to be thoroughly assessed to understand how the efficiency is determined by the environmental conditions and target species.

## Design of the Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG)

The Fish Spiral Sluice Gate (FSSG) was designed to provide a simple, compact solution for fish to overcome barriers between 1 m and 10 m high. It consists of three winded immobile “canals” shaped as a vertical Archimedes’ screw, each with an entry (i.e., the lower valves) and exit (i.e., the upper valves). The lower and upper valves are surrounded by an outflow chamber. Each canal has an artificial substratum from gravel that is glued on the Archimedes' screw, is completely filled with water and contains five pressure sensors: three throughout the canal, one at the entrance and one at the exit. The lower and upper valves are adjusted accordingly to the pressure inside of the canal. When the lower valve is fully opened then the upper valve opening is at its smallest. The main idea is for fish to be attracted by the flow at the lower valve when it starts to open, enter the system when the lower valve fully opens and make their way towards the upper valve, to then exit the “canal” when the upper valve opens.

## Aims

The aim of this study is to assess the **efficiency of the FSSG** and understand how fish of **different species and sizes** **respond** to its mechanisms. In doing so, recommendations can be formulated on how appropriate and feasible the use of the FSSG for fish passage would be under different conditions. The assessment was done via an experimental set-up under controlled conditions with real fish.

## Experimental set-up

As the FSSG is a relatively complex system, designed to enable safe passage via the subsequent opening of multiple valves, a traditional set-up in which fish are provided at the entrance and recaptured at the exit to determine mortality rate and nature of injuries, would be insufficient [@bierschenk2018]. To really understand the system and how it affects migrating fish, there are more questions to be answered than the general question: How many fish make it through the exit? More specifically, questions that need to be answered are: When do fish enter the FSSG when do they leave it, how much time (or cycles) does it take them to find the entrance and move up the FSSG, how does experience with the system alter fish behaviour and how does the fish size and species determine the passage efficiency?

The unique operating conditions of the FSSG and multiple questions to be answered, required an alternative assessment approach. In 2023 a pilot experiment was conducted to test different methodologies. Fyke experiments and pit telemetry experiments were evaluated and fine-tuned to come up with a sound methodology that was used during multiple experiments of 2024. The fyke experiments, which involved fish release and recapture, were found insufficient to provide sound insights. The PIT telemetry experiments on the other hand were found to be suitable and after some tests to optimize placement and detection probability, the methodology was fixed. To ensure for the reader a good overview of the final conclusions made with the fixed methodology, the PIT telemetry experiments of 2024 in combination with the most insightful PIT telemetry experiments of 2023 are discussed in depth. As they were crucial for the development of the used methodology and given the additional information they still hold, the fyke experiments and first PIT telemetry tests are described and discussed in the appendix.

## PIT (Passive Integrated Transponder) telemetry

PIT telemetry is a wildly used technology, enabling the tracking of fish or terrestrial animals, especially in narrow systems [@thorstad2013]. Similar to other telemetry techniques, it relies on a tag inserted or fixed on a fish but also on an antenna, which generates a magnetic field, charging the tag which then emits a response that can be read by the system [@bubb2002]. Two types of PIT telemetry exist: Half-Duplex (HDX) and Full-Duplex (FDX). In FDX systems, the antenna continuously generates a magnetic field and the tag response can constantly be detected and recorded. HDX systems switch between the “generating a magnetic field” mode and “reading tag response” mode. Antennae are simpler in HDX, can be larger and also require less power. They are made of a copper inductor wire wrapped as a loop, generating the magnetic field. This antenna is then connected to a tuning box, itself linked to a reader box where the data logging computer is [@barbour2011]. The tracked animal is usually tagged internally in the abdominal cavity with a different tag depending on whether the system is HDX or FDX. Tags of different sizes can be used, with the large ones having a strong signal and the smaller ones having a weaker signal. The signal range can be impacted by the presence of metal around the antennae, although it is often still usable. **HDX telemetry was used in the present study.**
